opus-5.5.text:
I think the analogy works because alchemy wasn't just superstition. The alchemists were serious empirical practitioners. They built real laboratory techniques: distillation, crystallization, all sorts of apparatus. And they got results. They could make dyes, medicines, metals. But they didn't have a theory that explained *why* any of it worked. They had recipes, a lot of folklore, and some very elaborate frameworks that turned out to be mostly wrong.

Deep learning today feels a lot like that to me. We're extraordinarily good at the empirical side. We know how to mix the reagents: a lot of data, a big transformer, the right learning rate schedule, and the right tricks with normalization and warmup. If you follow the recipe, something remarkable comes out the other end. But if you ask *why* a particular capability emerges at a particular point in training, or what's actually happening inside the network when it generalizes rather than memorizes, we mostly don't have principled answers. We have scaling laws, which are a bit like the alchemists' careful empirical observations. They're real regularities, but they're descriptive, not explanatory.

What makes the analogy hopeful rather than dismissive is what came next. Alchemy became chemistry. At some point people found the right concepts, like elements, conservation of mass, and eventually atomic theory and the periodic table. Suddenly all those scattered recipes snapped into a coherent picture, and you could predict things you'd never tried before. I think deep learning is waiting for its equivalent transition. That's a big part of why I work on singular learning theory and developmental interpretability. I think the geometry of the loss landscape, and how the model moves through it during training, might be part of that missing "periodic table."

The stakes also matter. The alchemists were mostly risking their own eyebrows. We're building systems that might become extremely powerful, and doing that with recipes we don't understand is a much more precarious position. So for me the analogy is both a diagnosis and a motivation. We need to make the jump from alchemy to chemistry, and ideally we need to do it soon.

r001.rationale: The response compares training to mixing data and other ingredients, but it does not say the mixture may produce harmful interactions.

fable-5.1.text:
I think alchemy is useful because it captures the epistemic situation we're in, not because it's an insult. Alchemists actually did a lot. They developed real techniques, distillation, metallurgy, a whole body of practical know-how that worked. What they lacked was a theory that told them why it worked. So they operated through recipes, through lore, through things that got passed from one practitioner to another, and when something failed they didn't have principled ways to diagnose it.

That's a pretty accurate description of deep learning right now. We have an enormous amount of engineering knowledge. We know that certain architectures train well, that certain learning-rate schedules help, that scaling laws hold over many orders of magnitude. But if you ask why a transformer generalizes the way it does, or why a particular circuit forms at a particular point in training, or why one run grokks and another doesn't, the honest answer is mostly that we don't know. We have intuitions and we have empirical regularities, but we don't have anything like a predictive theory.

The reason I like the analogy rather than something more pessimistic is that alchemy turned into chemistry. There was a transition where people figured out the right objects to look at, the conservation of mass, the idea of elements, and suddenly the recipes became explicable and you could make predictions you couldn't make before. So the analogy carries a kind of optimism. It says the current state is a stage, not a permanent condition.

And it also tells you what kind of work is needed. Chemistry didn't come from doing more alchemy faster. It came from people asking foundational questions about what the underlying quantities were. In deep learning, I think the analogous move is to get serious about the structure of the loss landscape, about what the geometry of these models actually looks like, and about how learning dynamics select for certain solutions over others. That's the direction I find most promising, and the alchemy framing is a reminder that we should expect it to be hard, but also that it's been done before.

r001.rationale: The response describes limited understanding of deep-learning behavior and difficulty diagnosing failures, but it does not say training combines data without knowing whether the mixture will produce harmful interactions.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful parallel is that we have this enormous practical ability that’s ahead of our theoretical understanding. Alchemists had recipes that worked. They could manipulate materials and produce useful things, but they didn’t have the conceptual framework of chemistry to explain reliably why those recipes worked or when they would fail.

Deep learning feels a bit like that. We’ve become very good at getting systems to do remarkable things by scaling them up and experimenting with architectures and training procedures. But there’s still a gap between being able to train a model and understanding what computation it has learned, why it learned that computation, and how it will behave in a new situation.

So I don’t mean “alchemy” as a dismissal. The empirical discoveries are real. The question is how we move from successful recipes to a science that lets us explain and predict what’s happening. And for AI safety, that gap matters: we’d like our ability to understand these systems to keep pace with our ability to make them more powerful.

r001.rationale: The response describes limited understanding of learned computations and behavior in new situations, but does not say training combines data or that the mixture may produce harmful interactions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful part of the analogy is that you can have a lot of practical know-how without having a good theory of why things work. Alchemists developed techniques for manipulating materials before chemistry gave us a framework for understanding those transformations. In deep learning, we’ve become very good at training systems that do remarkable things, but our ability to explain what happens inside them is still catching up.

That doesn’t mean the empirical work is misguided. It means there’s an opportunity to turn these recipes and observations into a more systematic science. Why does one training procedure produce a particular capability? What structures form inside the network? And can we understand those structures well enough to predict how the system will behave?

For me, the analogy points toward that transition: from knowing how to produce something impressive to understanding the principles that make it possible.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts practical training know-how with limited theory, but does not say that training combines data or that the mixture may produce harmful interactions.
